HOME / AIRCRAFT / SAILPLANE
THE ART OF SOARING

Sailplane.

Long wings, quiet air, and a close connection to the atmosphere. Sailplanes turn the movement of air into a way to explore the sky.

Family
Fixed-wing glider
Propulsion
Usually unpowered in soaring flight
Launch
Tow, winch, or self-launch system
Primary role
Sport and recreation
OverviewKey featuresHow it worksCommon usesQuestions
01 / THE BIG PICTURE

Meet the sailplane.

A sailplane is a glider optimized for efficient flight. It trades height for forward travel and can gain altitude when surrounding air rises faster than the aircraft sinks. Some designs include an auxiliary engine.

SPOT IT IN THE SKY

Look for exceptionally long, narrow wings, a small cockpit, and a slim fuselage with little frontal area.

02 / DESIGN DETAILS

What makes it different.

01

Long, slender wings

A high aspect ratio helps reduce induced drag and makes efficient gliding possible.

02

Streamlined fuselage

A narrow body minimizes resistance while accommodating one or more occupants.

03

Clear canopy

The canopy gives the pilot a broad view of the sky and surrounding terrain.

04

Airbrakes

Many sailplanes use airbrakes or spoilers to help control descent and landing approach.

03 / HOW IT WORKS

The engineering
behind the flight.

A glider descends through the air while its wings generate lift. Pilots can extend a flight by finding rising air, such as thermals, ridge lift, or atmospheric waves. Within suitable rising air, the aircraft can climb relative to the ground without powered thrust.

04 / IN THE REAL WORLD

Made for a mission.

  • Recreational soaring
  • Cross-country gliding and competition
  • Training in energy management and reading the atmosphere
CAPABILITIES & TRADEOFFS

Sailplanes are aerodynamically efficient and can fly quietly, but unpowered soaring depends strongly on atmospheric conditions. Pilots plan ahead to keep suitable landing options within reach.

05 / A CLOSER LOOK

Good questions.

How does a sailplane get into the air?

Common methods include an aerotow behind another airplane or a ground-based winch. Some sailplanes have engines for self-launching.

Can a glider climb without an engine?

Yes. It can gain altitude when it flies through air rising faster than its own sink rate.

This guide describes an aircraft category. Equipment, speed, range, capacity, and operating limitations vary by model and configuration. Categories can overlap: a propeller aircraft can also be a cargo plane or seaplane.
